summary: This informational memo clarifies how HTTP version numbers should be used and interpreted, since there was confusion about interoperability between implementations of different versions. It was replaced by RFC 7230.

eli5.summary: Rules for how two people who speak different editions of a language can still understand each other.

subtitle: Rules for how implementations of different HTTP versions can work together.

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 introduced version numbers to label message format and capabilities, but implementations disagreed on how to interpret them, leading to interoperability failures when clients and servers with different versions tried to communicate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2145 clarifies that the major version determines message format (so major version changes are breaking), while the minor version signals sender capabilities but does not change how receivers parse headers. It defines how proxies handle version numbers and how senders and receivers should choose which version to send.
tldr.outcome: This cleared up ambiguities in the HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1 specs, allowing mixed-version deployments to work reliably. It was replaced by RFC 7230, which consolidated HTTP message semantics.

facts.label: HTTP major versions
facts.value: 1 and 2 defined by this RFC era

today: RFC 2145 is an Informational RFC and has been obsoleted by RFC 7230, which consolidated HTTP message semantics and syntax. However, the principles of HTTP version negotiation documented here remain the foundation for how modern HTTP versions (1.1, 2, and 3) interoperate.

sections.title: The Version Number Problem
sections.content:
HTTP uses a <major>.<minor> numbering scheme. The RFC/1.1 spec says that a major version change signals a change to message format, while a minor version change adds features without changing the general parsing algorithm. In theory, this lets old and new implementations coexist.

In practice, confusion reigned. Some developers misinterpreted the versioning rules, leading to implementations that would fail or reject messages from different versions. For example, some HTTP/1.0 implementations would reject an HTTP/1.1 message, even though HTTP/1.1 was supposed to be backward-compatible. The RFC attempts to clarify the original intent and define a clear interoperability contract.
sections.eli5: Imagine two people, one speaking English from 1990 and one from 2020. The rules about what you need to understand to talk to each other were unclear, so they often gave up and stopped talking.

sections.title: The Versioning Rules
sections.content:
The core rule: the major version sent in a message MAY indicate how to interpret other header fields, but the minor version MUST NOT. This is the key difference. Major version is format-breaking; minor version is capability-labeling.

A corollary: an HTTP/1.1 message sent to an HTTP/1.0 recipient must still be a valid HTTP/1.0 message when all headers not defined in HTTP/1.0 are removed. This allows HTTP/1.1 to extend HTTP/1.0 without breaking it.

Another critical rule: if a receiver gets a header it does not recognize, it MUST ignore that header (not reject the message). This 'robustness principle' (from RFC 791) is fundamental to HTTP versioning: a receiver should be liberal in what it accepts.
sections.eli5: If you get a word you don't know, skip it and keep reading. Don't throw the whole book away just because you don't understand one word.

sections.title: Proxy Behavior and Version Handling
sections.content:
HTTP version numbers are hop-by-hop, not end-to-end. A proxy never forwards the version number from a client to a server or vice versa. Instead, it sends its own version number based on what it supports. A proxy implementing HTTP/1.1 or later must forward unknown headers unless they are protected by a Connection header (which marks them as hop-specific).

For compatibility between minor versions of the same major version (e.g., HTTP/1.0 vs HTTP/1.1), an implementation of HTTP/x.b sending to a recipient known to be HTTP/x.a (where a < b) MAY send headers not defined in HTTP/x.a, but MUST NOT depend on the recipient understanding them. For example, an HTTP/1.1 server may send a Cache-Control header to an HTTP/1.0 client (which will ignore it), but must never send Transfer-Encoding: chunked to an HTTP/1.0 client (which cannot parse it).
sections.eli5: A translator in a phone call doesn't pass on the language itself; each person speaks their own. And if one person uses a word the other doesn't know, the translator says it anyway, but doesn't expect it to be understood.

sections.title: Client and Server Version Selection
sections.content:
Clients should send the highest HTTP version they support, as long as the major version is no higher than what the server is known to support. The client MUST NOT send a version it is not at least conditionally compliant with. As a last resort, a client MAY send a lower version if it has determined that the server is buggy and requires it, but only after explicit detection of the bug.

Servers should send the highest version they support, with a major version less than or equal to the version received in the request. A server MUST NOT send a version it is not compliant with. A server MAY send a 505 (HTTP Version Not Supported) response if it cannot send a response using the client's major version. Like clients, servers MAY send a lower response version if they suspect or know the client is buggy, but this should not be the default behavior and SHOULD NOT be done for HTTP/1.1 or later requests.
sections.eli5: Unless you know the other person doesn't understand your language, speak the fanciest version you know. But if you figure out they are confused, you can slow down and simplify.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
Security mechanisms introduced in one HTTP version may depend on the proper interpretation of version numbers in older implementations. For example, if a security feature relies on parsing a header that older versions were supposed to ignore, and an older implementation incorrectly rejects the message instead of ignoring the header, the security guarantee breaks.

The rules in RFC 2145 help ensure that version number handling is consistent enough that security mechanisms remain effective across implementations, even when they span multiple HTTP versions.
sections.eli5: If a lock depends on someone ignoring a label they don't understand, everything falls apart if they throw the lock away instead.
